source.title: Effective Frontiers: A Unification of Neural Scaling Laws
source.authors: Jia-Xuan Zou; Zi-Xuan Gong; Ye Su; Huayi Tang; Yong Liu

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some equations and figure labels are flattened or garbled in the web text; the paper is not cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives scaling laws theoretically and tests them in a controlled synthetic task, using weighted reducible MSE loss rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study's own synthetic sweeps and its derived compute-allocation formulas bear on V1, V3 and part of V7. Results cited from Kaplan et al., Hoffmann et al. and other works are not recorded as rows. The paper's claims that frontiers look sharp, its theoretical intermediate results, and fit-line choices not presented as outcomes are not additional experimental rows.
record.test_reason: Its own synthetic sweeps (one-hot Zipf identity task, two-layer ReLU net, weighted MSE) give loss-vs-N, D and steps curves with fitted power-law exponents across tail indices α. This is a new, non-language setting, so the rows bear on V5 (power-law form outside text pretraining) and V7 (exponents depend on data), not on V1, which is about LM held-out cross-entropy. The Kaplan/Chinchilla allocation results are derivations, not measured fixed-compute sweeps.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also claim the scaling exponents are invariants set by data tail α and optimization bias β (β≈2). They suggest data pruning and curriculum learning could improve the exponents. They present the synthetic experiments as confirming the derived N, D and τ laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses an effective-frontier theory and a synthetic two-layer identity-mapping task with weighted MSE reducible loss, rather than language-model pretraining sweeps measured by held-out cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: Empirical fitted scaling exponents vary with the Zipf tail exponent α. The theoretical compute exponent also depends on α and the assumed optimization-bias exponent β. The two derived compute-optimal allocation regimes differ according to which bottlenecks are active.

fits_no_version.finding: Effective frontier k* scales as N^0.53, D^0.65 (theory 0.67) and steps with implied β≈2.03 at α=1.5 (Fig 4). Pattern-wise residual profiles show a sharp frontier (Fig 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learned-pattern frontier in Zipf rank space advances as a power of resources

fits_no_version.finding: Theoretical argument that Kaplan- and Chinchilla-style allocations are both equilibria of a max-bottleneck problem, with exponents set by α and β.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-optimal split depends on which bottleneck (optimization vs data coverage) is active

record.problems: Experiments use a controlled synthetic classification task, one two-layer architecture, and weighted MSE rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy. The reported ranges are limited (N 10 to 1000; D 1,000 to 100,000; steps 10^3 to 10^5); no uncertainty estimates, error bars, or controls are reported. The compute-optimal allocations are theoretical derivations, not empirical fixed-budget optimization results.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying result rows left out. The paper's discussion of sharp frontiers and its cited results from other studies are not separate reported resource-scaling outcomes.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining or held-out cross-entropy. The synthetic sweeps cover only about 2 decades per resource.
No extrapolation from small fits to much larger runs.
No empirical fixed-compute sweep of N/D splits; the allocations are derived only.
Single two-layer architecture; depth and width are not varied at fixed N.
No image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer experiments; only one synthetic Zipf identity task.
No test of fitting-method or parameter-counting choices. No comparison of published fits. Curvature is not analysed.

missing.what: Frontier exponents k*∝N^0.53, D^0.65 vs theory 0.67, and β≈2.03 from the τ slope. These allow checking the model-scaling prediction γ(α−1) against the observed N exponents of 0.11–0.17, which the paper does not do.
Inferred β per α ranges 1.65–2.49 (r11–r15 values), which is not constant, although the authors call it consistent.

record.verdict_notes: Relation is T3 because only toy synthetic experiments exist. Linking r1–r15 to V5 is a judgment call: a reviewer could instead treat them as fits_no_version, since a one-hot identity task is not among V5's named regimes. The vocabulary is K=1000 while N reaches 1000 (and 2000 in the D and τ sweeps), so capacity saturation could affect the N curves. There are no error bars or seeds. The paper's claim of 'perfect' agreement holds for D exponents; for N exponents it is unverified. Allocation results are not empirical.

versions.untested_parts: Tests parameter count, dataset sample count and training steps in a synthetic task; it does not test language-model pretraining or held-out cross-entropy.
No small-run fits are used to predict substantially larger runs.
Derives allocations for two assumed asymptotic regimes, but does not empirically optimize parameter/token allocations across fixed-compute runs or test actual language models.
Uses one two-layer architecture; does not compare depth, width or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated-data training comparison, fine-tuning or transfer evaluation.

Empirically varies the synthetic data-tail exponent and derives exponents depending on tail and optimization assumptions. It does not test fitting-method choices, disagreements between published fits, or curves bending away from a single power law.

rows.subject: two-layer neural network with a bottleneck
rows.size_stated: Hidden dimension N varies from 10 to 1000
rows.operation_detail: Varied hidden dimension N and fitted log reducible loss against log N by linear regression.
rows.measure: Weighted reducible loss ΔL; fitted parameter-scaling exponent magnitude
rows.locator: Appendix B.1, Figure 6(a), tail index α = 1.3
rows.note: The plotted fit label gives the exponent magnitude; the loss curve decreases with N. This is a synthetic MSE task, not language-model cross-entropy.
rows.check: Toy MSE network, not a language model, so it does not bear on V1. Loss falls as fitted N^-0.11 over N=10–1000 (about 2 decades). Theory predicts γ(α−1) with γ≈0.53 (Fig 4), about 0.16 at α=1.3; the paper never compares the two.

rows.subject: effective-frontier framework
rows.operation_detail: Derived a fixed-compute parameter allocation by balancing capacity and optimization bottlenecks in the data-abundant regime.
rows.note: This is a derived result under the stated framework and assumptions, not an empirical fixed-compute sweep.
rows.check: This is an analytic derivation under the max-bottleneck assumption, not a measured result, so 'observed' is wrong. No exponent values are given and no fixed-compute runs exist.

rows.subject: effective-frontier framework
rows.operation_detail: Derived a fixed-compute parameter allocation by balancing capacity and data-coverage bottlenecks in the data-limited regime.

conditions.value: data-limited; D ∝ C/N; τ assumed sufficient to cover D

rows.note: This is a derived result under the stated framework and assumptions, not an empirical fixed-compute sweep.
rows.check: This is a derivation, not a measurement. The equal Chinchilla split follows only if αN=αD, which the paper does not show. Labelling Chinchilla as 'data-constrained' is the authors' framing.

relationships.condition: Synthetic one-hot Zipf identity task, two-layer ReLU net, MSE, α 1.3–2.1
relationships.reason: Reducible loss follows power-law fits in N, D and steps at every α (r1–r15). Ranges are only about 2 decades each.
relationships.display_finding: Reducible loss follows power-law fits along all three axes at every tested α from 1.3 to 2.1, over about two decades per axis.

relationships.condition: Varying data tail exponent α in the synthetic task
relationships.reason: Fitted exponents shift systematically with α: N 0.11→0.17 (r1–r5), D 0.24→0.55 (r6–r10), steps 0.14→0.21 (r11–r15).
relationships.display_finding: Varying the data-tail exponent shifted fitted model-size exponents from 0.11 to 0.17, data exponents from 0.24 to 0.55, and step exponents from 0.14 to 0.21.
